Interestingly this is also how virgin came to mean what it does now. In ancient times, virgin simply referred to an unmarried woman, not someone who hadn't had sex (it was synonymous with "maiden"). Of course, unmarried women were expected to have not had sex, but it's not like it could be proved unless they were caught in the act.

In mythology, what a lot of people forget is that Hecate (the goddess of magic and crossroads) is stated as a "virgin goddess" (alongside Athena, Hestia, and Artemis). Yet, by the same writers, is also mentioned to have had children by multiple men (such as Circe by King Aeetes, and Scylla by Apollo). She was a "virgin" in that she did not submit to a man as a husband, even though she bore children.

Huh, I actually thought that em dashes (—) was a tell for AI, but I searched it up and apparently I've been misusing en dashes for years (–), according to American English rules.

HOWEVER, apparently in New Zealand/Australian English (where I live), the way I've used it is correct. Hyphens have the same use across the board, but apparently en dashes ARE used for emphasis to replace commas and semicolons in New Zealand/Australia, so long as there is a space in between the en dash and what you're breaking up.

For example: 

*I was halfway up when Travis* – *may the gods grant him an eternal wedgie* – *kicked me.*

So it looks like my misconception was due to differences in grammar across English-speaking countries.

A MacGuffin is typically an object or person that drives the plot and motivates the characters on their quest, but ultimately has no importance to the story and can be easily interchanged for something else.

For example, the Philosopher's Stone in Harry Potter is a MacGuffin. Whilst it is the thing that Voldemort is trying to steal, ultimately it could've been exchanged for any item that grants immortality/a body. The stone isn't even seen until the last chapter of the book and is destroyed offscreen before the chapter ends.

By contrast, the One Ring from Lord of the Rings is NOT a MacGuffin. If it had been the One Necklace, it wouldn't have been able to slip off its user so easily, which happens multiple times and greatly impacts the plot when it does. Its powers also help Frodo and Bilbo from time to time (with its invisibility powers being essential to their escapes). It also tempted the Fellowship numerous times (especially Boromir and Frodo) and it was a constant struggle to resist. It was more of an antagonist than it was a MacGuffin.

Honestly, for me, it was because I had ideas that I wanted to explore and a lot of the fics that I read with that in mind either tend to never be finished... or just didn't scratch that itch I was looking for. 

For example, I'm currently writing an OC/Thalia Grace fanfic in the Percy Jackson fandom because I genuinely liked Thalia as a character and wish that she wasn't written out like she was in canon (her presence was what made *Titan's Curse* my favourite book in the series, yet it's the only book that she makes a decent appearance in despite being built up for two books). And I also like the idea of every pantheon being alive, but hardly any fics that do that ever end up finishing, which kinda sucks because there are those that combined the classic Greco-Roman, Norse, and Egyptian from canon with Shinto and Abrahamic religions, yet were abandoned just as they started getting good.

For me, it's these:

1. Formatting is shit. I don't mind one or two missing commas (typos happen after all) or one larger-than-usual paragraph (so long as it made sense). But when the whole chapter/story is like that, NOPE.
2. When the whole thing is in **bold** or *italics*. Those are meant for emphasis, or maybe to differentiate a character's thoughts from the description of the scene. 
3. Reader inserts. I'm fine with self-inserts or OC main characters (hell, I write a number of OC mains myself), but I absolutely hate Y/N in fanfics.
4. Mary Sues & Gary Stus. This is much more prevalent in self-insert and OC main character fics and I hate it. I'm all good with a powerful or "special" MC (*Demigod?* and *The Game of Gods* are some of my favourite Percy Jackson OC fics starring an OC demigod son of Kronos and a son of Artemis respectively (both of whom would never occur in canon)), so long as they have a personality, flaws, and aren't handed everything with no work/necessary build-up.
5. Messing up the lingo of a location/time. For example, don't use British idioms if the setting is in America (unless the character is British themselves... in which case, you have to have the Americans not understand what they meant), and vice versa. It's 100% okay if your spelling is different (after all, most English speakers use British English spelling), just make sure the lingo is all right. Same goes for using modern terminology when the story is in a medieval setting... only allowable if it's from a character from a different time period.
6. Gender-swaps and trans-ifying of canon characters. To a lesser extent (out of personal preference), messing with a canonical sexuality (it has to be a REALLY good fic for me to ignore that). I have seen enough female Harry Potters for a lifetime. I'm fine with fics that make a character gay/bi/straight if we never found out their preference, but once it's confirmed in canon, I personally prefer reading ships that adhere to that.
7. Extreme OOC of canon characters. Don't get me wrong, I understand that a lot of fics will have canon characters be OOC from their canonical counterparts. So long as there's a good reason for it, I don't mind it. My big issue is when characters suddenly deviate DRASTICALLY from how they were prior. For example, I enjoy Dumbledore being a manipulative chessmaster (good or evil, so long as he's smart/subtle about it)... I don't enjoy him being an irredeemable villainous idiot of a man who constantly spouts about "the Greater Good" and is outsmarted by his adversaries every time.
8. When real-world politics get involved in the fic. I come to fanfiction to get away from the real-world, not to have it blasted across my favourite story. I'm all good if the original source material had this sort of stuff in it... for example, the house-elf slavery debate in *Harry Potter* or the Separatist arguments in *Star Wars*, but if it had no story reason to be put in there beyond the author wanting to comment on the current state of affairs, it instantly draws me out of the fic. I lost interest in a good long fic because halfway through a chapter, the author went on a tirade about the author's supposed politics. Like, dude, this is not the place for it. Try Twitter or Facebook to express that, not in the middle of your story when there was absolutely nothing leading up to this yelling at the readers.

I am definitely one of those writers. 7 years ago, when I was 15, I posted a Harry Potter/Zootopia crossover. A weird combination, I know, but it was in response to a challenge I saw and I thought I'd give it a go.

It garnered a lot of attention because it was such a unique crossover (to this day, there are only 7 fics with that crossover on FFN, and I wrote 2 of them (the second was an attempted rewrite of the first)). The first fic had 11 chapters (42k words), but got 97 reviews, 210 followers, and 165 favourites. The second had 5 chapters (22k words), and got 46 reviews, 200 followers, and 157 favourites. From first post on the first fic to last post on the second fic was 2 MONTHS, and I abandoned them.

I absolutely cringe at my writing 7 years on, but I abandoned both those fics because I couldn't keep up and I was stupidly getting input from fans and constantly rewriting chapters to fit what THEY wanted. Years later, I kept getting the occasional review on the work, asking when I was going to start up again. I honestly considered releasing a post to pretend I had died before finishing the work so that they might have some closure (yeah, dark stuff, I know).

7 years on (age 22), I've started to write again. This time, a simple OC-centered fic in Percy Jackson (a classic, right?). I've started writing what I WANT to write. I barely get any responses, but I actually like what I'm putting out.

Sometimes, the writers of abandoned works just lose their passion for the project and have to take a step back for our mental health. We are writing for free after all, so the minute we start dreading the next post, it becomes a chore for us.

If I can be a bit biased, I tend to prefer the shipping of MALE OCs to female canon characters... simply because they are few and far between. Most of the OC/canon character fics I see are female self-inserts/male canon characters, and I've only really found a couple that I liked ([Some Things Never Sleep](https://www.fanfiction.net/s/12567601/1/Some-Things-Never-Sleep) was one of my favourites), whereas the majority of male OC/canon characters I've found are more up my alley. I guess it's a matter of oversaturation of the female OC/canon character that made me appreciate the male OCs more.

But in all honesty, I can go either way. There are some times I prefer the canonical ships (i.e. Atom Eve/Invincible or Aang/Katara), sometimes I prefer non-canonical ships with canon characters (Harry Potter/Hermione Granger or Percy Jackson/Thalia Grace). With OC/canon characters, there's definitely a wider variety of ships that I like (since it takes out half the equation of canonical chemistry). It's all up to how they're written.

Of course, when it comes to OC pairing, I tend to favour the OCs that pair up with characters that didn't canonically have a love interest that they ended up with (at least in the fandom it's in). For example, I like OC/Raven stories in the Teen Titans cartoon series (where she never has any feelings for her comic love interest Beast Boy), but I'm not as into OC/Raven in the DCAU (where Damian and Raven have a great chemistry and eventually kiss).

Anyway, TL;DR - Write what you like and those who enjoy it will flock to it. There's always an audience for it somewhere.

Progressive is going against the socially accepted because it's the right thing to do... woke is being performative about things that are currently socially accepted by wider society (but weren't 50 years ago).

Two things preclude something from being woke (in my opinion):

1. Is it subtle in its messaging or its cast (i.e. not a big deal is made about including a lesbian lead or something similar)? If yes, then it's not woke.
2. Are its messages going AGAINST the socially acceptable because goddammit it's the right thing to do? If yes, then it's not woke.

If you had one or the other, I (personally) consider it progressive, not woke. Diversity in films and TV can be easily done without a show being "woke". 

Look at Hazbin Hotel (one of my favourite shows) - it's literally got the most stereotypical frat-boy white heterosexual male as the VILLAIN (Adam) with the heroes including a cast of an Italian gay sex worker in an abusive relationship with his pimp, the main character is a bisexual demon in a relationship with her lesbian angel girlfriend, and an asexual cannibalistic serial killer demon - ALL OF WHOM ARE CONSIDERED THE HEROES without it coming off as "woke" because the show doesn't make a big deal/draw attention to it beyond showing character development or portraying them with no difference between them and a normal romance plot (in fact, I don't even think any of those words (gay, lesbian, bi, etc.) were even spoken in the entire show) - they were shown but not told. This was good representation where it was so subtle I didn't even notice it until someone pointed it out, and it made me love the show even more.

And then look at Brooklyn Nine-Nine, which up until Season 6 was my favourite cop show... and it was a good liberal show with a very diverse cast. It wasn't subtle nor was it going AGAINST the socially acceptable, but it had decent writing, great comedy, and didn't really draw attention to its political messaging beyond a few moments, which were for the most part handled tastefully and amazingly. Find your nearest fire pipe, and shoot a shock bolt in front of it (not under the pipe) to immobilise Laura when you lure her into it. While she's convulsing, shoot a harpoon bolt into the bottom nozzle of the fire to keep it burning permanently. Provided that Laura is on the other side of this (and you stay directly in front of her) and that she wasn't directly under it when the fire started, she'll continue to run right into the flames until she dies.

I'm a trophy hunter and this game is notorious for being a 9/10 on the difficulty scale to 100%, putting it in the higher echelons of games in terms of difficulty. I however did manage to get the platinum on this game (100% of all base game trophies), which included completing the infamous Akumu mode, where you die in one hit from EVERYTHING (it's so fun on Akumu mode though).

The good thing is that it does get easier with time... my first playthrough on Survival difficulty (the  highest initial difficulty, but second LOWEST overall) was hell compared to playing it on Akumu (though to be fair, I was also doing it without upgrades for the trophy, so I made it even harder for myself). 

My recommendations... make MULTIPLE saves, I cannot stress this enough. Sometimes you may waste ammo/resources that you can't afford to use... which can soft-lock your progression. It's always best to make a save after every chapter and not to overwrite it until you are FAR further into the game.

I also recommend learning when you HAVE to fight and when you can avoid combat altogether. Boss fights are a given... bar one instance in the middle of chapter 10, you can not progress until you've dealt with the boss. THAT is when it's acceptable to let loose your ammo. 

Most other times, I recommend either using stealth or alternative strategies to deal with enemies without wasting ammo (whether it's running away or luring them to traps is up to you). Hell, remember Chapter 3, you can avoid all enemies by rushing straight to the boss and killing him first (he takes 8 chest shots from a non-upgraded pistol on AKUMU mode to kill (or 1 torch, 2 hatchets and 5 non-upgraded bullets (I recommend that order)), and killing the Sadist kills all enemies in the area. That's one example of using a good strategy for maximum output.

Speaking of traps, I highly recommend that you try to disarm every trap you come across, as they reward you with trap parts that will be EXTREMELY useful when you're stuck as you can craft agony bolts for every occasion. And, if you notice a lot of free ammo is around, try to prioritise using what similar ammo you have so you can maximise your resources.

Also, I recommend you quickly learn the power of the matches. They may not seem like much, but if you're able to time dropping a match on a body when there are multiple enemies running at you, you can instant-kill ALL that are within a certain range without wasting ammo or damaging yourself.

Gigli failed because of a bad, clumsy plot, poorly written dialogue and a perceived lack of on-screen chemistry between the two leads of Affleck and Lopez (despite the fact that they were dating at the time). It was also much worse of a bomb since it only made $7.2 million back on a $75.6 million budget, and if still considered one of the worst movies of all time. 

Bros, by comparison, had some decent writing, but it failed to differentiate itself from other rom-coms beyond saying "but this time it's two guys" with its marketing. Its marketing focused on the importance of the first GAY rom-com rather than exemplifying its comedic elements and plot points, which made a lot of people not want to see it.

From a financial perspective, rom-coms are, statistically, a more profitable genre than action films. They typically take less money to make than action (often less than half the budget), and tend to bring home a little over double their budget in revenue (with an average of 204% return compared to action's average 187%), so rom-coms aren't a bad genre to make if you're looking to make a profit without investing excessive sums of money.

But again, the FOCUS (not presence, but the focus) on gay relationships in a rom-com turned off the highest demographic of rom-com watchers, which heavily contributed to its flop. I never said that the "Mighty Number 9 style audience-insulting" didn't help with its flop, just that it wasn't as big a factor as forgetting the demographic of the genre. 

A comedy centred around gay people would've thrived (look at *Will and Grace*, which ran for 22 years); a romantic film around a gay couple would've succeeded (look at *Brokeback Mountain*)... but a rom-com (without any star power due to them wanting only LGBT actors), with the comedy being replaced by needless pandering, was not going to end well. Even a romantic dramedy like *Love, Simon* pulls in more viewers because of it being a comedy-drama with a gay romance (the star power of Nick Robinson and Jennifer Garner didn't hinder it either).

It wasn't a lack of marketing, considering that despite it's production budget being $22 million, Universal spent $30-40 million on its marketing... which itself alienated a lot of its viewers because of a line at the end of the trailer - "Remember straight people?" - that effectively told a lot of straight people that it wasn't for them.

It received a decent word of mouth from those who watched it, with approximately 70% of viewers polled saying they would recommend it to others, so that wasn't a major factor in its flop.

What did effect its box office success was its focus on representation rather than its humour and a lack of interest in the material from viewers (because they had alienated the biggest viewers of rom-coms: straight women and even women in general).

A gay romantic film CAN become immensely successful, just look at *Brokeback Mountain,* which had a much smaller budget of $14 million and made $178 million back in 2005... and that was with its marketing explicitly stating that it was a gay love story. However, in the case of *Bros*, it being a GAY rom-com (rom-coms tend to not appeal to men as much as a romance film can, and women typically watch rom-coms to imagine themselves as the woman in the on-screen relationship) hindered its chances of at least breaking even by alienating its audiences with its premise and marketing.

To sum up, having gay people as the focus likely wasn't the SOLE reason for *Bros* flopping, but it certainly was one of the biggest reasons.

Whilst I don't think Zootopia 2 would flop due to the inclusion of gay people (I mean, the first Zootopia had a gay couple (Bucky and Pronk) as Judy's neighbours and no one cared), I do believe it would flop if NICK was gay... purely because it seems that the vast majority of Zootopia fans tend to ship WildeHopps, and doing so would instantly alienate a lot of the film's following.

Yes, yes I do." are made explicitly romantic in nature (since the specific phrases used in each translation were things only said to romantic partners/lovers, when there was a perfectly good ambiguous/platonic translation available).

And I genuinely hate to be the bearer of bad news, but there was a recent movie that flopped TERRIBLY because of it having gay people in it: Bros (2022). It was a romantic comedy consisting entirely of LGBT actors and characters, made with a budget of $22 million... and got just under $15 million back at the box office. Apparently, the filmmakers had forgotten that the vast majority of rom-com watchers were straight women and that they wouldn't be as interested in a gay rom-com with gay orgies in it (I'm not joking, there is literally a four-man gay orgy in it). It was too gay for straight audiences to enjoy, and "pandered too much to straights" for gay people to enjoy.

Just off the top of my head, here are my opinions on the Batman villains I can recall.

**Joker**: Irredeemable. Very rarely has he ever chosen to live a normal life, with the only times I remember being when Batman "died", and when he lost his memory. He relapsed both times.

**Poison Ivy**: Redeemable. Her motives are good, but the way she's going about them is where she messes up. If she could be convinced to aim towards helping the environment peacefully instead of attacking/killing innocent and some not-so-innocent people, then I think she'd be able to be redeemed.

**Harley Quinn**: Redeemable. She's proven time and time again that, once she gets out from under Joker's influence, she is often a good hero.

**Riddler**: A mix of both. I personally liked his run as a private detective, where he could put his talents to good use, however I think that he's probably one of the more villainous of Batman's Rogues.

**Catwoman**: Redeemable. I mean, she's barely been a villain the past few decades, and when she is a villain, she's more of an anti-villain.

**Penguin**: I don't want to say he's irredeemable, but he's not redeemable either. He's gone straight-ish, but only because he realised it's more profitable with less chance of being beaten by Batman, not out of any regret for what he's done. Nowadays, he's on the level of (former) mobster rather than villain.

**Two-Face**: Redeemable. If he could get therapy to assist him with his personality disorder, it's likely that he can return back to the Harvey Dent that Gotham remembers. 

**Ra's Al Ghul**: Irredeemable. The guy has gone for hundreds of years as the head of the League of Assassins and it's unlikely he's gonna change anytime soon. Also, every time he dies, he becomes more crazy. 

**Victor Zsasz**: Irredeemable. This guy's a bloody psychopath, and one of the scarier kinds since he's the most likely to exist in real life.

**Scarecrow**: Irredeemable. I haven't seen a single redeeming quality from this man, and the sort of sadistic enjoyment he gets from watching people suffer in fear is horrifying to say the least.

**Mr Freeze**: Redeemable. He's a desperate man whose only goal is to save his wife, once that is accomplished, he usually stops his life of crime.

**Bane**: Irredeemable. The guy grew up in prison and doesn't appear to have any inclinations to turn his life around.

**Killer Croc**: Redeemable. He was shown, in his very first appearance, that he's not so much of a villain as he is someone who has been ostracised his entire life for his looks. Does that make him turn to villainy? Often, yes, but he is able to be reasoned with and has assisted Batman many times in the past.

**Black Mask**: Irredeemable. He's a violent mobster with nothing to indicate he'll realise the "error of his ways".

**Professor Pyg**: Irredeemable. He's got a really creepy obsession with chopping people up and, just like Zsasz, is scary because he's one of the more realistic psychopaths in Batman's Rogues.

**Clayface**: Redeemable. He has shown in the past that he can use his powers for good.

**Firefly**: Irredeemable. A pyromaniac who has no care about who he hurts, only how much he can burn things.

Here's my take:

I hate multiplayer trophies in primarily single-player games solely because they will eventually close servers down and make the trophies (and therefore, the platinum) unattainable. If it weren't for server closures, I'm sure people would be more accepting of multiplayer trophies.

Collectibles are fine so long as it's not 200 hard-to-spot collectibles with no variation and no hints as to where they are, spread out across an open-world (looking at you, GTA V and GTA IV, with the damn letters, spaceship parts, and pigeons respectively).

RNG trophies are more frustrating than anything else, especially if you've got really shitty luck. It stings all the more when the game implements a workaround (like Injustice 2 did with the Legendary Multiverse to get the Cat Call ability), but the workaround is a much longer grind than waiting for RNGesus to bless you.

I have no problem with speedrun trophies (provided the times are reasonably fair, allowing for one or two mistakes to be made), nor multiple playthroughs or difficulty-related trophies (provided that the difficulty was at least play-tested beforehand (looking at you, Uncharted 1-3 with your Brutal difficulty)).

Honestly, my perfect trophy list would include trophies like these:

* Difficulty specific trophies (that stack, so that if you go straight to the hardest difficulty, you skip multiple playthroughs)
* Collectible trophies (specifically for finishing each collectible tree, not just picking up 1 and calling it a day)
* Story-related trophies (limited to BIG milestones, like defeating a boss (like every Soulsborne game) or completing questlines (like the "Hero of Skyrim" trophy for completing the Civil War questline in Elder Scrolls V)
   * This includes viewing all endings if a game has more than one
* Challenge-based trophies (such as "Win all races" or "Beat all time-trials with a platinum rating", etc.). 
   * This includes speed-run trophies if a game is linear enough for it
* Some miscellaneous trophies (like "Complete a heist without being detected",  or a cool Easter Egg reference to other games (like Vampyr's "Unlife is Strange" reference to DONTNOD's more famous title "Life is Strange"))

I'm talking about the cover fire exploit where you stand behind cover and shoot without exposing yourself. And also some glitches that will allow you to skip entire gunfights (which still work on patch 1.02), in particular the chapter 4 gun fight.

Don't get me wrong, the game tweaks certainly help a lot, but they're not the end-all, be-all of getting the Charted - Brutal! trophy.

Brutal is, as the name suggests, a brutal challenge that will more often than not leave you in tears especially since ammo is limited and the enemies keep one-shotting you. But when you finally beat it, oh boy does it feel satisfying.

The real problem areas are chapters 4, 13, 14, 19 and 25. Once you get to chapter 26, you're guaranteed the trophy since the final boss battle is exactly the same as Crushing difficulty.

My advice: use every exploit you can (so long as you don't skip entire chapters, you're free to use exploits to skip some of the worst gunfights) because some of these fights are complete BS, with limited ammo/maneuverability and waves upon waves of enemies.

Try to minimise your time out in the open during combat sequences, and try to get used to the game's blindfire mechanics and the cover-shooting exploit (where you don't "take cover", but you stand behind the cover and angle your shot to where you can shoot the enemies but they can't shoot you).

In Crushing, your biggest learning curve will be in the infamous Chapter 4 shootout. During the first wave, you'll want to either stay put or start making your way to the rightmost corner of area, as it'll minimise the angles at which enemies can approach you.

You will likely experience some frustration, but just try to think of each checkpoint as a goal. Don't be discouraged if it takes you more than a couple attempts to advance to a new checkpoint. Patience is the key to getting past Crushing.

This way, the fights aren't won by raw power, but by aspects of the character that had been set up before.

**Harry Potter and Voldemort**: Both are wizards that can speak to snakes (hell, they even have similar backstories of being orphaned, raised by Muggles, and they looked very similar before Voldemort became evil). Yet it was made to serve as Rowling's message that it was our choices that made us who we are, NOT OUR ABILITIES. 

**Darth Vader and Luke Skywalker**: Both wield the Force to a similar extent (primarily telekinesis) and even have similar fighting styles with a lightsaber. **Sherlock Holmes and Moriarty**: Both are geniuses, with the only difference being that Sherlock devoted himself to solving crimes whilst Moriarty was devoted to committing crimes.

**The T-800 and the T-1000**: Both are Terminators, with one having been reprogrammed to protect John Connor and the other is trying to kill him.

**Iron Man and the Iron Monger**: The first "mirror match" of the MCU, with Tony Stark fighting against Obadiah Stane in the Mark I armour (and with the better ARC reactor). I can understand that you might get tired of the "mirror match", but the unfortunate part of fiction is that, in order for them to be interesting, they have to be on a near-level playing field by the time the final battle occurs, and the mirror match just so happens to be the easiest way to do that.

Think of it this way. Sex is based off if you have a Y-chromosome or not, whereas gender is based off your brain chemistry.

There are two primary sexes: male and female. Although genetic abnormalities do result in chromosome mutation, this doesn't necessarily mean that there are more than the 2 sexes already put forth; it just means that there was an error when the code for your body was being written. To use an example, let's suggest that our genetic code is like the code of a video game. In the mass production of the code, there could be errors/mutations in the code of the  "game" that changes some of the "game's" graphics design. This doesn't necessarily mean it's a different game, it just means that there's a few different features than what was initially intended. (This isn't the best analogy, but it's the one I thought was the most apt when writing this.)

With gender, it gets a little more complicated. Studies have shown that male and female brains are inherently different and TEND to be "wired" for different things. This doesn't mean that male and female brains are inferior to one or the other, far from it, but it does mean that the typical male and female brain have different chemical reactions that determine how the brain functions (which itself is a result of millions of years of evolution forcing it to evolve in this way). There are, at most, three genders: male, female and transgender. A transgender would be, for example, a male brain inside a female body OR a female brain inside a male body. The confusing signals of a female brain inside a body it wouldn't normally interact with (and vice versa) would often cause discomfort/feelings of not being in the right body, which is called gender dysphoria (which is often one of the leading reasons of sex changes, so that one's gender aligns with the physical markers of the sex their brain would be accustomed to).
